title: Squares, Square Roots, Cubes, Cube Roots and Exponents
shortDescription: Perfect squares/cubes, root methods, unit-digit patterns, exponent laws and surds.
genZNote: Memorise squares to 30 and cubes to 15 once — they save more time than any shortcut.

sections.heading: Squares and Square Roots
bullets: (a ± b)² = a² ± 2ab + b²; (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
Perfect squares end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 — never in 2, 3, 7, 8.
Square root by prime factorisation or division method; for 4-digit squares, use unit digit and nearest square. √1764 = 42.
Sum of first n squares = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; sum of first n odd numbers = n².

sections.heading: Cubes and Cube Roots
bullets: Cube root unit digit mapping: last digit of cube 1→1, 8→2, 7→3, 4→4, 5→5, 6→6, 3→7, 2→8, 9→9. ∛2744 = 14.
(a + b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³; a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²).

sections.heading: Exponents and Surds
bullets: aᵐ·aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(p/q) = (qth root of a)ᵖ.
Unit digit cycles: 2, 3, 7, 8 repeat in 4s; 4 and 9 in 2s; 0, 1, 5, 6 fixed. Example: 7¹²³ → cycle 7, 9, 3, 1; 123 mod 4 = 3 → 3.
Surds: rationalise by multiplying by the conjugate: 1/(√a + √b) = (√a − √b)/(a − b).

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Squares, cubes and exponents rely on memorised values, identities and unit-digit patterns for speed.

highYieldFacts: Sum of first n odd numbers = n².
commonTraps: Do not forget negative exponents flip the fraction.
